core.title: Use colon for hierarchy and dot for variant in artifact names
core.given: An artifact name whose colon (:) and dot (.) separators carry meaning
core.when: the artifact name is chosen, referenced or reviewed
core.then: Use colon (:) only for hierarchical descent to a deeper conceptual level, and dot (.) only for a lateral variation (flavor/state) of the same thing.
prefer: Colon for each step deeper into the resource tree; depth is unlimited.
Keep dots shallow: typically one dot suffix for a variant of the same artifact, rarely two.
avoid: Chaining multiple dots (e.g. .uuid.v7.encoded) — this usually signals over-specification.
Using a dot to express a deeper conceptual level, or a colon to express a mere flavor/state of the same thing.
core.why: Colon is a strong boundary between different conceptual levels; dot is a soft boundary between facets at the same level. Keeping them distinct makes names navigable as a tree and keeps variants shallow.
evidence: Every colon in the artifact names in scope separates a different conceptual level (deeper in the resource tree).
Every dot segment denotes a flavor/state of the same thing at the same level.
Dot usage is shallow per the advisory guidance: typically one dot, rarely two; names with multiple dots are inspected as a likely sign of over-specification (warning, not a hard limit).
verification: Check that every colon in an artifact name separates a different conceptual level (purpose = hierarchical descent, multiplicity unlimited, strong boundary between conceptual levels) and that every dot segment is a lateral variation of the same thing at the same level (purpose = lateral variation, soft boundary between facets of the same level).

Warning heuristic: an artifact name with two or more dots (e.g. .uuid.v7.encoded) usually indicates over-specification — emit a warning, not a hard failure; this is advisory, not a validity ceiling, so no hard dot-count limit is enforced.
Deciding whether a segment is a deeper conceptual level or a variant of the same thing is a semantic judgement: an automated check covers separator counts and shapes, not the meaning of segments.

Scope: applies only to artifact names — dots in file names, file extensions or code-level identifiers, and colons in prose or in the key/value syntax of data or configuration files that are not part of an artifact name, are out of scope.

values: artifact name containing ':' or '.' separators added, changed or referenced
separator misused (colon for a variant, dot for a deeper level)

fires: A new artifact name is introduced for a nested concept, one colon step per deeper conceptual level.
A state or flavor of an existing artifact is named (e.g. a raw form or an active state) and the dot separator must be chosen.
An existing or referenced artifact name chains several dots (e.g. .uuid.v7.encoded) and is reviewed for over-specification.
A review checks whether existing artifact names use colon and dot with their intended meaning.
doesNotFire: Work that neither names, references nor reviews artifact names.
Dots inside file names, file extensions, or code-level identifiers that are not artifact names.
Colons in prose or in the key/value syntax of data or configuration files that are not part of an artifact name.

neutralityNotes: The convention is already stack-neutral: it governs separator semantics of artifact names and names no stack, runtime, framework, language, package manager, file suffix or path, so the core needs no profile data (profileRequirements empty, nothing to propose). Concrete example names (commons:ux:foundations:color, sensory:gesture.raw, ...) and the verifier's example set stay in the Bun realization (bunOnly); the generic .uuid.v7.encoded illustration was kept because it names no stack. Two neutralizations: doesNotFire's 'YAML key/value syntax' became 'key/value syntax of data or configuration files' (YAML is the Bun stack's plan-artifact markup; instantiated with Bun the same cases are covered), and fires[0]'s 'e.g. a foundation under commons' became the generic nested-concept wording ('commons' is the stack's layout concept). Activation fact notes are not part of the core fact schema; their content (the two-or-more-dots warning observer; the semantic-judgement limitation) is preserved in core.verification. The 'typically one dot, rarely two' guidance stays advisory — no hard ceiling was added — and unless is empty in bun.json and remains empty in the core, so no exception was dropped or added.
